n2.topic: What happens if you correct someone in the meeting when they present your idea as theirs
n2.why_it_hooks: A clear point of tension that most people have lived through. It lays out the best case, the worst case and the likely case, then gives three levels of script: in the moment, right after the meeting, and in a written follow-up that puts your name on the idea.

n2.topic: 'Never disagree with your boss in public' is too blunt: how to disagree in a meeting without a fight
n2.why_it_hooks: It reframes a rule many people take literally. The verdict is tweak, with three scripts: asking a question that exposes the issue, adding a risk, and offering an alternative. It also covers when private really is better.

n2.topic: What happens if you reply to a rejection email and ask for feedback
n2.why_it_hooks: It's a free move almost nobody makes. The video is honest that most replies are generic or absent, shows how to phrase the ask so it's easy to answer, and covers the odd case where it reopens the door.

n2.topic: 'References available upon request' is wasting a line of your resume: what to use that space for
n2.why_it_hooks: A short, specific, easily checked tip that viewers can act on in one minute. The verdict is bin, with a list of what to use the space for instead, including a skills line, a link, and targeted keywords drawn from the job posting.

n2.topic: Rewrite It Live: a Slack message that just says 'Hey, got a minute?'
n2.why_it_hooks: It is relatable and a little funny. The video rewrites it into a message that states the topic, the urgency and the time needed, so the other person can reply asynchronously. It also shows when a quick call is still the better option.

n2.topic: What happens if you ask for a promotion outside the review cycle
n2.why_it_hooks: People assume they have to wait until review season. The video covers the best case, worst case and most likely case, explains why asking for a 'path conversation' gets more traction than asking for a title, and gives the opening script and a one-page evidence list.

n2.topic: When the interviewer says 'Any questions for us?', here are five questions that signal you're a serious candidate, and one to avoid
n2.why_it_hooks: Everyone gets this moment and most people waste it. The video gives a verdict on the popular 'ask about culture' advice, then offers sharper questions with the reasoning behind each, such as what success looks like at 90 days and what the last person in the role did well.

n2.topic: Rewrite It Live: the 'sorry for the delay' email that makes you sound junior
n2.why_it_hooks: A habit nearly every viewer has, and the fix is small and concrete. The video swaps apology for 'thanks for your patience', and shows where a genuine apology is still right. It runs through a line-by-line rewrite of a late reply.

n2.topic: What happens if you turn off work notifications after hours without telling anyone
n2.why_it_hooks: It speaks to burnout and the fear of looking disengaged. It looks at the realistic outcomes, then gives a script for setting expectations on response times and for handling a real emergency, so you protect your evenings without looking absent.

n1.topic: What happens if you stay in Zone 3 instead of Zone 1 in London: a day-by-day walk-through of the Tube/Elizabeth line commute, contactless fare capping, extra minutes each way and what the hotel saving actually buys you
n1.why_it_hooks: It turns the vague 'stay outside the center' question into minutes, cost and stress. The twist is that the answer depends on which line your hotel is on, not on the zone number.

n1.topic: Heathrow to central London, three ways: Heathrow Express vs Elizabeth line vs Piccadilly line. Door-to-door time, cost, luggage hassle, and which to pick by arrival hour and hotel area
n1.why_it_hooks: Almost everyone landing in London has to make this choice. The surprise is how small the time gap is compared with the price gap for many hotel locations.

n1.topic: 36 hours in San Francisco with a parent who can't do hills: a flat-route plan using the Embarcadero, Ferry Building, Crissy Field and the Presidio, with a 'we deliberately left out' list that includes Lombard Street and Alcatraz
n1.why_it_hooks: A group-type constraint that nearly every guide ignores. SF's reputation for hills is real, so the plan feels both practical and personal.

n1.topic: Rainy-day Vancouver that beats the sunny-day plan: Granville Island Public Market, the Museum of Anthropology at UBC, and covered transit links, with walking times between stops
n1.why_it_hooks: Vancouver's rain is well known, and most visitors arrive with no plan B. Framing the wet plan as the better plan fits the channel's core promise.

n1.topic: Melbourne or Sydney for a first 4-day Australia city break? A simple framework: weather by month, walkability, food vs landmarks, and cost of getting around, ending in a clear pick by traveller type
n1.why_it_hooks: Readers genuinely struggle to choose between these two. A framework with a clear verdict by traveller type beats a 'both are great' comparison.

n1.topic: How many Smithsonian museums fit in one day in Washington DC? A realistic two-museum cap, walking times along the Mall, a lunch plan, and how to check which museums need free timed-entry passes
n1.why_it_hooks: Free entry tempts people to cram in six museums. The video shows the real maths of time and tired feet, and proves that less is better.

n1.topic: Skip It / Swap It: London. Madame Tussauds, the Changing of the Guard at Buckingham Palace, the London Eye, Camden Market on a Saturday, and Oxford Street shopping. Each gets a verdict and a swap such as the Horse Guards ceremony or a Thames walk.
n1.why_it_hooks: It targets tourist staples that people feel obliged to do. Offering a specific alternative for each one makes it a decision tool rather than a rant.

n1.topic: Toronto Pearson to downtown: UP Express vs TTC vs rideshare at rush hour. Real time ranges, cost, where each drops you, and which neighborhoods make each option the best choice
n1.why_it_hooks: The UP Express is a fast, fixed-time train, while road traffic into the city is unpredictable. Readers get a clear rule for choosing based on arrival time.

n1.topic: 48 hours in Quebec City in January: a cold-weather plan with indoor warm-up stops every 60-90 minutes, a realistic daylight schedule, and a list of outdoor things we deliberately left out
n1.why_it_hooks: Winter city breaks scare people off. Building the schedule around warm-up stops makes the cold feel manageable, and the topic is seasonal and specific.

n1.topic: What happens if you turn up in Edinburgh in August without booking a bed: Fringe-season price spikes, the options that remain, how far out you end up, and what the commute does to your trip
n1.why_it_hooks: It builds on the Edinburgh topic that already worked, but changes the angle from weather to timing. It shows a booking-window mistake with concrete outcomes in cost and stress.

n1.topic: What to skip in San Francisco and what to do instead: Fisherman's Wharf, Pier 39, a last-minute Alcatraz plan, driving down Lombard Street, and a Golden Gate Bridge walk in morning fog. Verdicts include when to book ahead.
n1.why_it_hooks: Alcatraz tickets are known to sell out in advance, so 'do it, but only if you book early' is a surprising and useful verdict. Fog on the bridge is a real issue that is rarely planned for.
